summary.text: Electron diffraction is the bending and scattering of electron beams caused by elastic interactions with atoms, with no change in the electrons' energy.
The electrons are scattered by Coulomb forces from the atomic cores and surrounding electrons, and the map of their outgoing directions is a diffraction pattern.
It works because matter can act as a wave, and it is used in electron microscopes and in several techniques for studying crystals, surfaces and molecules.

facts.label: Typical sample
facts.value: A thin slice, from 1 to 100 nanometers thick

facts.label: Type of scattering
facts.value: Elastic, meaning the electrons keep their energy

facts.label: Orientation matters
facts.value: Patterns depend strongly on how the crystal sits relative to the beam

facts.label: Surface techniques
facts.value: Low-energy electrons give LEED, used to study surfaces

facts.label: Simple model
facts.value: Uses the de Broglie wavelength and often Bragg's law

items.prompt: An electron passes close to an atom and is deflected, but leaves with exactly the same energy it came in with. What kind of scattering is this?

options.label: Inelastic scattering, since the direction changed
Elastic scattering, since the energy stayed the same
Absorption, since the atom took the electron in
Emission, since the atom produced a new electron

items.explain: Electron diffraction comes from elastic scattering, where there is no change in the energy of the electrons.

items.prompt: What pushes an electron off course as it passes through a sample?

options.label: Gravity pulling toward the heaviest atom nearby
Magnetic forces from the sample's thin edges
Electric forces from the atomic cores and surrounding electrons
Pressure from the surrounding air molecules

items.explain: Electrons are scattered by Coulomb forces from both the positively charged atomic core and the negatively charged electrons around the atoms.

items.prompt: A researcher rotates a small crystal slightly in the electron beam and the spots in the pattern change a lot. What does this show?

options.label: The pattern depends strongly on crystal orientation relative to the wave
The crystal has been destroyed by the beam
The electrons have lost all their energy
Electron patterns never depend on the sample at all

items.explain: There is a strong dependence on the relative orientation of the crystal and the incoming wave.

items.prompt: Young's two-slit demonstration shows a wave getting stronger in some directions and weaker in others. How does this connect to electron diffraction?

options.label: It shows slits are always required for an electron beam
It proves electrons are heavier than any light waves
It shows light is made of electrons stuck in slits
Crystal atoms act like many small points that diffract the wave

items.explain: With a number of small points in place of slits, similar effects occur, comparable to an electron wave diffracting from atoms in a small crystal.

items.prompt: A simple geometric model of electron diffraction gives where spots appear. Why might scientists need a fuller model?

options.label: The simple model gives the geometry but not accurate spot intensities
The simple model cannot say anything about direction
Fuller models are only needed for light, not electrons
Simple models predict that no spots appear at all

items.explain: Simple models give only the geometry of the intensities; dynamical diffraction is needed to calculate more accurate intensities and spot positions.

items.prompt: Why can't we notice wave-like behavior in a thrown tennis ball, even if all matter can be thought of as waves?

options.label: Tennis balls are not made of matter
The wave-like behavior of macroscopic objects is impossible to measure
Waves only exist for objects smaller than a crystal
Tennis balls cancel out their own waves by moving

items.explain: All matter can be thought of as matter waves, but it is impossible to measure any wave-like behavior of macroscopic objects.
